director.chapterArc: A shift from weary routine to a chilling tactical realization; Rook's silence becomes an admission of prior knowledge, shifting Toren's trust into dread.
director.restraintNote: Maintain the 'neutral observer' stance throughout. The horror is in what Rook *didn't* say and how he moved, not in shouting or melodrama. Let the final realization land with a drop in pace rather than an increase in volume.

cues.delivery: Senna's voice is dry and practical; she treats the pain as a logistical problem to be solved. No whining, just sharp instruction.
cues.through: "Then move the water can, Wyck Tanner, and stop lying on my legs, because I can't feel them properly and I need to be able to tell you the truth about whether you're on them."

cues.delivery: Toren's complaint is sullen but measured; Rook's agreement is flat and factual.
cues.from: "It's not the same," he said on the second morning. "You're a man with a stick. It's not the same thing at all."
cues.through: "It isn't," Rook agreed. "It's about a fortieth of the same thing. Do it again."

cues.delivery: Rook's final line is a command; sharp and immediate.
cues.from: "And then twice a week until one of us is dead," Rook said. "Go."
cues.through: "And then twice a week until one of us is dead," Rook said. "Go."

cues.delivery: Cass Ordway's voice is weathered and direct; she speaks with the flatness of someone who has seen too much. Rook remains still.
cues.through: "Hah." It was not a laugh. It was the noise a person makes when a thing adds up. She came the rest of the way in and the boy came with her, and Toren noticed that she stopped eight feet out and slightly to one side, which was almost exactly where Rook made them stand. "Right. Then you'll want this and you won't like it. Coldharbour's gone."

cues.delivery: The revelation of 'men' rather than monsters must be delivered with absolute clarity. The shift from fear to dread is in the silence.
cues.through: "The ones that call themselves Cinder Company," said Cass Ordway.

cues.delivery: Rook's questions are tactical; his voice loses its flatness only in the subtext of urgency. Cass is defensive.
cues.through: "The shed," Rook said. "And the kiln house. Did they put them to the torch or did they go through them."

cues.delivery: Narrator must slow down here to let the weight of Rook's question land. The silence is heavy.
cues.from: It was not the words. Toren replayed it for years and it was never the words. It was that Rook asked it in a voice with the flat gone out of it — not raised, not hurried, but with a thing underneath it that had not been there in the previous three questions and had not been there at any point in nineteen days.

cues.delivery: Cass's observation is sharp; Rook's departure is abrupt and final.
cues.from: "You've asked me four questions," she said, "and not one of them was is there anything left worth taking."
cues.through: And he walked north past both of them without one further word.

cues.delivery: Toren's observation is quiet; Rook's confirmation is brief.
Rook's analysis is clinical and precise; he speaks to the group but his focus is on the evidence.
cues.from: "There was a gate here." The posts still stood; the gate itself lay flat in the mud eight feet inside. "Off the hinges and inward, so it was pushed, and it was pushed from the lane side. That's the first thing that happened and it happened before anything else, because there's nothing on top of it and everything else that's been dropped in this yard has been dropped on the mud beside it."
cues.through: "They took the boards, and they took whatever lived in that." Rook nodded at a shelf under the beam, where a rectangle of clean dry board sat in the middle of ten years of lime dust. "That's a book. That's a book that came out and went back every working day for a long time."

cues.delivery: Rook's explanation of the book is delivered with a sense of grim value; he treats it as cold fact.
cues.from: "Where they hunted," said Rook. "What came out of which ground, on what day, in what numbers. A hunting outfit's book is nine years of where the country is turning and where it isn't, and there is no other way to get that information except to go and stand in it for nine years." He wiped the dust off his hand. "It's worth more than the ash and it doesn't weigh anything."
cues.through: "They did this before," he said, "and they'll do it again, and whoever's running them knows exactly what they're for."

cues.delivery: Rook's voice is quiet and detached; Milo's reaction is internalized.
cues.through: Rook walked past him and went to get water.

cues.delivery: Rook's movement is fast but controlled; his dialogue to Toren is firm and dismissive of the boy's panic.
cues.from: He did not ask for it and he did not put his hand out and wait. He crossed nine feet of wet stone and took it out of a boy's open palm, and Toren's hand was still open and still up in front of him a full second after the thing had gone out of it.
cues.through: "Put the cart above the kiln, please," Rook said, "and then come back down and help me with the bins, because we are not leaving four hundredweight of ash standing in a yard for the next people down this road, and I would like it under a tarpaulin before dark."

cues.delivery: Wyck's confrontation is low and steady; Rook's evasion is calm but firm. The tension comes from the silence between lines.
cues.from: "That's not a name you were hearing for the first time."
cues.through: "North-east in the morning," he said. "Everybody sleeps. I'll take the whole watch."

cues.delivery: Toren's internal monologue slows significantly. The final realization must be delivered with a drop in pitch and pace.
cues.from: Toren lay awake in the dark and made himself go through it the way Rook had taught them to go through a piece of ground.
cues.through: He didn't work it out. He recognized it.

pauses.reason: Completed thought; transition to narrator observation.

Major emotional landing; the silence after 'No' is critical.

pauses.after: Toren stood on the wharf edge in the wet gray and looked at four hundredweight of Riftspawn ash lying in open bins under a roof, with the lids stacked neatly against the wall where somebody had put them down, and understood the size of what he was looking at better than any amount of explaining could have given him. He had carried three flasks of that stuff to a factor's scale and got twelve measures for it and been told it was a very good take.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; the realization of what they are looking at.
Emphasis on the specific detail of the gate damage.
Isolation of the book's true value.
Pause for the weight of the ritual silence.

pauses.after: Rook turned the chit over once. The rain came down on the wharf. Down the basin a moorhen went across the open water and made its noise, and Milo said something to Dessa about the shed, and none of it reached the nine feet of stone Toren was standing on.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; Rook's action with the chit is a pivot point.
Emphasis on the action that shifts Toren's perception.

pauses.before: Is it toward them or away from them?
pauses.reason: Full pause before Dessa asks the critical question of direction.

pauses.after: Rook got up and put the fire out with his boot, which was two hours before he had said he would, and stood in the dark above a wharf where seven people had worked and five were under stones, looking down the lane at the gate that had been pushed inward off its hinges by somebody standing on the outside.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset; shift from dialogue to final scene setting.
Emphasis on the logical deduction Toren is making.

pauses.after: You would put three men across a gate so that nobody in the yard could use it.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing; the realization of Rook's knowledge.
